title: Prisons expose the hypocrisy of American freedom
subtitle: American free market capitalism leads to an unfree society
author: David Garland
introduction: America claims to be a nation built on freedom that views state intrusion into individual liberty as the ultimate tyranny – so why does it have the world’s largest prison population? NYU law professor David Garland argues that this clash between a professed love of liberty and a massive apparatus of confinement is the logical outcome of the country’s political economy. Rather than prioritising dignity and flourishing, America’s freedom has always centred around markets, and free markets need a penal state to control the wreckage that they leave behind.
body:
In the early 1830s, Alexis de Tocqueville, the first and still best-known theorist of American society, formulated a paradox about the young nation. America was, he said, a land “of the most extended liberty” and yet its prisons “offer the spectacle of the most complete despotism.” Freedom and unfreedom were juxtaposed in a way that surprised the French visitor and struck him as ironic.

Nearly two centuries later, commentators still find it puzzling that liberal America deploys its penal power more extensively and intensively than any other country in the world. How could America, that storied land of liberty, be home to mass incarceration, police killings, and racialized law enforcement? How could it be a comparative outlier on virtually every dimension of criminal justice.

In a recent book, entitled Law and Order Leviathan: America’s Extraordinary Regime of Policing and Punishment, Iargue that there is nothing paradoxical about America’s reliance upon a massive penal state. The liberalism characterizing modern America is, first and foremost, an economic liberalism, dedicated to “free enterprise” and the free rein of market forces rather than a political liberalism concerned with the dignity and flourishing of every individual.

Rather than protect all from each, as in the Hobbesian social contract, America’s penal state provides protection to some groups and some places while oppressing and excluding others.

Since the collapse of the New Deal order in the 1970s, the nation’s politics have been dominated by a tough-minded market fundamentalism that empowers corporations and the business class; renders working families insecure; holds individuals responsible for their fate; and pays little heed to the liberty interests of poor people—particularly if they are Black and accused of a crime. In such a system, extensive penal control is a corollary of the nation’s values—not a contradiction. If there is a tension between America’s social arrangements and the fact of mass incarceration, it exists chiefly in the domain of ideology and national self-regard—and we know from the history of slavery and segregation that ideological dissonance of that sort can be tolerated for long periods of time.

Capitalism is always a socially disruptive force, and historically it has been especially disruptive in the US, where comparatively few restraints have been imposed on corporate power and market forces. In American cities between the 1970s and the early 1990s, these long-standing conditions were dramatically intensified first by deindustrialization, then by the retrenchment of federal urban policy, and finally by a resurgent, “free market” capitalism that generated levels of social disorganization, disorder, and violence rarely witnessed in the developed world.

In the face of this disorder, and against a background of deepening economic insecurity, a substantial part of the American electorate came to fear crime and violence—and threats to their property values—more than they feared the illiberal use of state power. The result was a new kind of social contract between Americans and their government: a “law and order” covenant in which voters repeatedly gave their consent to policies promising public safety through penal control.

It wasn’t from a Hobbesian state of nature that this penal Leviathan emerged, but from a peculiarly American state of insecurity that flowed directly from the political economy of late 20th century American capitalism. Rather than protect all from each, as in the Hobbesian social contract, America’s penal state provides protection to some groups and some places while oppressing and excluding others. This was the repressive, racialized regime of policing and punishment that the protests of summer 2020 exposed, and, for a brief time, made to seem intolerable.

***

Criminal law enforcement is always and everywhere prone to excess and injustice. But Americans, above all poor Black Americans, are subject to exceptional levels of police violence, incarceration, and penal control that exist nowhere else in the developed world, and these sit alongside levels of homicide, armed robbery, and gun crime that are equally exceptional. This demands explanation, not because it contradicts the nation’s “liberal” ideology, but because, as a comparative matter, it is extraordinary.

These linked phenomena were generated by specific historical processes operating within a specific social structure. America’s economic arrangements weaken the social controls of civil society—disorganizing communities and families—which generates extraordinary levels of criminal violence; and predisposes government to adopt penal control as its standard response. In other nations—and in affluent America—these informal social controls are the foundation of social order and the primary prophylactic against crime. In America’s poor neighborhoods, especially segregated, inner-city neighborhoods where most residents are poor and Black, these informal controls atrophy for lack of support and resources. That same political economy reinforces a pattern of racial division, social distance, and interpersonal distrust that allows most Americans, most of the time, to turn a blind eye to the harmful effects of aggressive policing and penal control.

America’s political economy is also extraordinary—both in terms of the labor market’s primary distributions and the secondary distributions of its tax code and welfare state. Compared to other affluent nations, America exhibits greater inequality, more economic insecurity, more precarious and low-paid employment, fewer workers’ rights, and higher levels of poverty and material deprivation. Its levels of child poverty, infant mortality, untreated mental illness, drug-related death, single-parent households, teenage pregnancies, housing and health insecurity, high school non-completion, and deaths from homicide are the worst, or among the worst, in the developed world. Homicide levels today are around half of what they were in the 1980s and 1990s—the decades when today’s penal state was built—but even at that lower level, they are still 5-8 times as high as those of other developed nations.

America’s political economy exposes communities, families, and individuals to greater market-generated risks, while its welfare state provides them with fewer social protections—a situation exacerbated by economic and political shifts that occurred after the 1960s. The result, in cities all across the country, from the late 1960s to the early ’90s, was extraordinarily high levels of social disorganization and violent crime. These problems were dealt with not by economic investment and social provision—as in the War on Poverty—but by economic abandonment, aggressive policing and harsh penal control.

***

Political economy forms the core of this theory, but this doesn’t imply any neglect of the causal significance of race. On the contrary: racial hierarchies, racial legacies, and racist assumptions are woven into the fabric of America’s political economy and are routinely reproduced by its structures and processes. Racist assumptions are also woven into American culture, and these tropes and connotations are frequently challenged and countered by the forces of anti-racism. By comparison, the racism of political economy goes unremarked. In the theoretical models of social science, “race,” “economics,” and “politics,” are often conceived of as discrete, independent variables that can be studied separately. But, in reality, and in reality-congruent theory, these are interwoven dimensions of complex social processes, power relations, and institutional arrangements that have been developed and reproduced over long stretches of historical time.

Structural explanations can be overly abstract and deterministic, invoking anonymous, inexorable forces to explain the conduct of lawbreakers, penal agents, or politicians. I want to stress that the structures of political economy impact places, communities, and families in observable, tangible ways—chiefly by controlling the flow of resources and the opportunities to which people have access. But “political economy” alone is not a complete explanation of the penal state: crime rates cannot be simply read off from political economy; and nor can criminal justice policies.

America’s dual epidemics of criminal violence and penal control have their roots in the socio-economic circumstances in which so many poor people live—conditions caused by the larger structures of political economy.

Local demographics, politics, and policy choices all shape how—and how far—these structural pressures are expressed, which is why America’s homicide rates, its rates of police killings, and its rates of imprisonment, though always well above the average for developed nations, have varied over time and across the 50 states within what I will call “the American bandwidth.” Three things produce this variation:  differences in political economy across time and space, local differences in demographics, politics, and policies; and intermediating processes that mitigate or aggravate the effects of political economy on patterns of crime, policing, and punishment.

Penal states—and the power they project through policing, punishment, and penal control—function in most developed nations as essential but relatively minor back-up mechanisms supporting the positive controls of civil society. In the routine course of social life, individual conduct is steered towards norms of good order by various means—by the self-controls and pro-social values that individuals internalize in the course of their upbringing; by law-abiding behaviors modeled by families, peers, and neighbors; and by the prompts, incentives, and controls that operate in schools, communities, workplaces, and social life more generally. The penal controls of the state are always present, but they mostly stand in the background of social life, activated only when mainstream institutions break down and fail to secure adequate levels of compliance. Crime control is, most of the time, a mainstream social achievement, routinely produced—rather than the result of the state’s policing and punishment. In that sense, the criminal justice system is to crime control what the welfare state is to people’s welfare—that is to say, marginal, supplementary, and remedial. Most people, most of the time, have their welfare needs met by virtue of employment or family networks, and state welfare operates as a supplement or backstop, not the primary provider. Similarly, most crime control results from socialization and informal social control, not from the threat of penal sanctions.

These processes are not, however, automatic. They depend on the existence of high-functioning, well-resourced institutions. Nor are they uniformly accomplished across time and space. In America, because of the destabilizing effects of market forces on certain groups and certain places, mainstream processes of social control are often weakened or undermined—to a point where they fail to regulate individuals and establish orderly communities. This failure can lead to social disorganization, crime, and violence, all seriously aggravated by the widespread availability of guns. When this occurred in America between the mid-1960s and the mid-1990s, it triggered political processes that, over the course of several decades, resulted in the formation of an extraordinary penal state.

***

What marks the United States off from other nations in these respects is not negative attitudes towards criminals; nor racist attitudes towards minorities. It is the distinctive material circumstances in which these attitudes are brought to bear—the “social background” against which US crime control and criminal justice operate.

Politicians, policy makers, and control agents in American cities behave differently than their equivalents elsewhere not, or not simply, because they are more racist, or punitive, or inhumane. They behave differently because the problems they face, and the choices available to them, are shaped by socio-economic circumstances that are quite different from those of other developed nations. Perceptions of these circumstances are, no doubt, overlaid by ideologies and stereotypes; interpreted using institutional scripts; and approached in ways that may be unnecessarily risk-averse. But the fact that America’s material realities are so different must be accorded a central place in any theory of the penal state.

America’s dual epidemics of criminal violence and penal control have their roots in the socio-economic circumstances in which so many poor people live—conditions caused by the larger structures of political economy (and exacerbated by the ubiquity of guns). These conditions diminish the social control capacities of communities; they increase pressures for offenders to engage in violence; and they prompt officials to embrace aggressive tactics.

A theory that grounds the penal state in political economy is not a single-factor explanation. It is a structural account, in which a complex field of human action (the penal state and its practices) is explained by showing how it is patterned by a complex set of institutional arrangements and structural forces (political economy), but also by intermediate, neighborhood-level, processes and local policy choices that are patterned by structural forces but not fully determined by them.

In our daily lives, we do not see, or feel, “structures” or “structural forces”—the concept refers to a theoretical abstraction rather than a lived experience. The result is that people do not ordinarily think in terms of structures, and when they do, they tend to simplify how they operate—especially when applying structural reasoning to crime and criminal justice. People on the Left tend to overstate the effects of structures, forgetting there are always various responses to even the most forceful of structural pressures. People on the Right make the opposite error, flatly denying the effects of socio-economic structures and insisting on a version of free-will voluntarism and individual responsibility that is as harshly blaming as it is sociologically untenable. Against these misleading abstractions, it is important to specify concrete, observable processes that link macro-structures to micro-outcomes; and to recognize that while individual choice always exists, it is often radically constrained by the circumstances within which it is exercised.

Contrary to what some latter-day Tocquevillians suggest, the illiberalism of America’s penal state is neither paradoxical nor anomalous. It is a social trait with deep roots in the nation’s history and in the structures of its political economy, which is why no one who has spent any time in the United States is really shocked to learn about mass incarceration, about police violence, or about the pervasive racism of the penal state.
